title: The Pearl Syncussion SY-1
intro: The Syncussion is Pearl’s drum synthesizer of 1979, the drum company’s answer to the Syndrum. It was sold with a pair of pads to strike, and its two channels made the falling toms, lasers and metallic hits of late-1970s disco. It led towards the electronic drum kits of the 1980s.

timeline.name: Pollard Syndrum
timeline.text: The first commercial drum synthesizer: an oscillator struck from a pad, with a pitch sweep and a decay. Its falling tom spread through disco.

timeline.name: Pearl Syncussion SY-1
timeline.text: Two channels, each two oscillators with six ways of combining them, a pitch sweep, an LFO, a sample and hold and a filter swept by the decay, played from Pearl’s CU-1 pads with dynamics from how hard they are hit.

timeline.name: Simmons SDS-V
timeline.text: The hexagonal-pad Simmons kit, which took electronic drums from an effect to a whole drum set. The Syncussion is often named as a forerunner.

timeline.name: Pearl Drum-X DRX-1
timeline.text: Pearl’s own follow-up: a five-voice analogue kit in a rack brain, with programmable kits.

timeline.name: Behringer SYNCUSSION SY-1
timeline.text: The Syncussion’s circuit with its two channels side by side, separate outputs, trigger, tune and mute sockets, MIDI and a Eurorack-sized case. Announced in 2021, shipped in 2024.

relatives.name: Pollard Syndrum
relatives.text: The drum synthesizer it answered, with the same struck, sweeping voice.

relatives.name: Simmons SDS-V
relatives.text: The electronic kit that followed, with a voice per drum.

relatives.name: Behringer SYNCUSSION SY-1
relatives.text: A modern recreation of the same circuit, also in the app.

note: None of the databank’s records name the Syncussion yet. Its sounds here are in the general style of disco and electro percussion, not copies of parts.
